name: Hydrochloric acid
solubility: miscible
description: Strong monoprotic acid. It dissociates completely in water, so a 1 M solution has a pH close to 0. Reacts with reactive metals to release hydrogen gas, and with carbonates to release carbon dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solution density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Hydrochloric acid

name: Sodium hydroxide
solubility: very soluble (about 109 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Strong base, also called caustic soda. It dissociates completely in water, so a 1 M solution has a pH close to 14. Feels soapy on skin because it attacks skin tissue — it is not safe to touch.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility, solution density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium hydroxide

name: Sodium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 36 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Common table salt dissolved in water. The salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so its solution is neutral. Present as separate Na plus and Cl minus ions in solution.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility, solution density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium chloride

name: Copper(II) sulfate solution
solubility: soluble (about 20 g per 100 mL at 20 °C, anhydrous)
description: Bright blue solution. The colour comes from the hydrated copper(II) ion. Slightly acidic because the copper ion reacts weakly with water. Used to demonstrate displacement by more reactive metals such as zinc and iron.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Copper(II) sulfate

name: Lead(II) nitrate solution
solubility: soluble (about 52 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution of a soluble lead salt. Lead compounds are cumulative poisons and must never be tasted, touched, or poured down a drain. Used with potassium iodide to show the formation of a bright yellow precipitate.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Lead(II) nitrate

name: Potassium iodide solution
solubility: very soluble (about 148 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution of a very soluble iodide salt. The salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so its solution is neutral. Supplies iodide ions for precipitation reactions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium iodide

name: Silver nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 216 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution used as the standard test for halide ions. Leaves dark brown or black stains on skin and clothing that take days to wear off. Kept in a dark bottle because light slowly decomposes it.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Silver nitrate

name: Phenolphthalein indicator
solubility: insoluble in water, soluble in ethanol
description: Acid-base indicator supplied as a solution in ethanol. Colourless in acidic and neutral solution, turning pink above about pH 8.3. Used to find the end point of a titration. The solution itself has no meaningful pH of its own, so pH is left empty.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, indicator transition range); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Phenolphthalein

name: Distilled water
solubility: not applicable
description: Water with dissolved salts and minerals removed by distillation. Used to make up solutions and to rinse apparatus. Freshly distilled water is neutral at pH 7, though it slowly turns slightly acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density at 4 °C); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Water

name: Zinc metal
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Bluish-grey metal, supplied as granules or strips. More reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution. Reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen gas. Being a solid metal it has no pH, so pH is left empty.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Zinc

name: Sodium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 36 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Ordinary salt dissolved in water, formed when an acid and an alkali neutralise each other. Neutral, colourless, and a good conductor because it is fully split into ions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium chloride

name: Water
solubility: not applicable
description: Water formed as a product of a reaction, most often when an acid neutralises an alkali. Neutral, and a very poor conductor on its own because it has almost no free ions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Water

name: Lead(II) iodide
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.08 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Bright yellow solid that appears when a soluble lead salt meets a soluble iodide. It is almost insoluble in cold water, so it drops out of the solution as a precipitate. Being a solid it has no pH of its own, and it does not conduct because its ions are locked in place rather than free to move.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Lead(II) iodide

name: Potassium nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 38 g per 100 mL at 25 °C)
description: Colourless solution left behind when lead nitrate reacts with potassium iodide. The salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so it is neutral, and it conducts well.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium nitrate

name: Silver chloride
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.0002 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White curdy solid formed in the standard test for chloride ions. Almost completely insoluble, so it appears as a precipitate. Left in sunlight it slowly darkens to grey as light breaks it down into silver metal.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Silver chloride

name: Sodium nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 88 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left in the tube after silver nitrate reacts with sodium chloride. Neutral, fully dissolved, and a good conductor.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium nitrate

name: Zinc chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 395 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution formed when zinc dissolves in hydrochloric acid. Mildly acidic rather than neutral, because the zinc ion reacts weakly with water.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Zinc chloride

name: Hydrogen
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 1.6 mg per litre at 20 °C)
description: Colourless, odourless gas given off when a reactive metal dissolves in an acid. It burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with air, which is why a flame must be kept well away. It is the lightest of all gases.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Hydrogen

name: Magnesium ribbon
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Light silvery metal supplied as a thin ribbon, usually with a dull oxide coating that is cleaned off with sandpaper before use. High in the reactivity series: it fizzes vigorously in dilute acid and displaces less reactive metals such as zinc, iron and copper from their salt solutions. It barely reacts with cold water but reacts readily with steam.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity

name: Iron filings
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Grey magnetic metal supplied as filings so it has plenty of surface area to react. It sits above copper but below zinc in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate but cannot displace zinc. Its solutions in this lab are iron(II), which are pale green.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity

name: Copper turnings
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Reddish-brown metal. It sits BELOW hydrogen in the reactivity series, which is why it does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid at all and gives off no hydrogen. It is also the metal that appears as a red-brown coating when a more reactive metal is put into copper(II) sulfate solution.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity

name: Calcium granules
solubility: insoluble in water (it reacts with it instead)
description: Soft silvery-white metal of Group 2. Unlike magnesium it reacts steadily with cold water, giving off hydrogen and leaving a cloudy white suspension of calcium hydroxide. It is stored away from moisture because it reacts with water vapour in the air.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity

name: Zinc sulfate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 58 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left behind when zinc displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate, or when zinc dissolves in dilute sulfuric acid. The loss of the blue colour is the clearest sign that the copper has left the solution. Mildly acidic because the zinc ion reacts weakly with water.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Zinc sulfate

name: Iron(II) sulfate solution
solubility: soluble (about 30 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Pale green solution formed when iron displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution. Watching blue turn to pale green is how this displacement is recognised. It is distinctly acidic because the iron(II) ion reacts with water, and it slowly turns yellow-brown in air as iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III).
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(II) sulfate

name: Magnesium sulfate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 35 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution formed when magnesium displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate. Known outside the laboratory as Epsom salt. Very close to neutral, just slightly on the acidic side, because magnesium hydroxide is only a weak base.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Magnesium sulfate

name: Magnesium chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 54 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left when magnesium dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid. Slightly acidic rather than neutral, because magnesium hydroxide is a weak base while hydrochloric acid is strong.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Magnesium chloride

name: Iron(II) chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 65 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Pale green solution formed when iron dissolves slowly in dilute hydrochloric acid. Acidic because the iron(II) ion reacts with water. Like iron(II) sulfate it is slowly oxidised in air towards yellow-brown iron(III).
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(II) chloride

name: Calcium hydroxide solution (limewater)
solubility: only slightly soluble (about 0.17 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The saturated solution of calcium hydroxide, known as limewater. Strongly alkaline even though very little of it dissolves. Because so little dissolves, any excess stays as a white cloudiness rather than going into solution. Limewater turning milky is the standard test for carbon dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Calcium hydroxide

name: Magnesium oxide
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 0.006 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White powdery solid formed when magnesium burns in air or reacts with steam. It is a basic oxide: the little that dissolves makes the water alkaline, and it neutralises acids to give a salt and water. Being an insoluble solid with its ions locked in place, it does not conduct electricity.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Magnesium oxide

name: Sulfuric acid
solubility: miscible
description: Strong dibasic acid — each molecule can give away two hydrogen ions, so it neutralises twice as much alkali as the same amount of hydrochloric acid. Its salts are the sulfates. Concentrated sulfuric acid also removes water from other substances, which is why it chars paper and sugar, but the dilute acid used here behaves as an ordinary strong acid.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solution density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sulfuric acid

name: Nitric acid
solubility: miscible
description: Strong monobasic acid whose salts are the nitrates, all of which are soluble in water. It is also an oxidising agent, which is why its reaction with metals usually gives oxides of nitrogen rather than hydrogen. It stains skin and fingernails yellow.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solution density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Nitric acid

name: Sodium carbonate solution
solubility: soluble (about 21 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Also called washing soda. The salt of a strong base and a weak acid, so its solution is distinctly alkaline even though it contains no hydroxide in the bottle. Fizzes with any acid, giving off carbon dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium carbonate

name: Calcium carbonate (marble chips)
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.0013 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White insoluble solid found in nature as marble, limestone and chalk, and used in the laboratory as chips because they react at a steady, watchable rate. Fizzes with acids to give carbon dioxide. It is also the white solid that makes limewater turn milky in the test for carbon dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Calcium carbonate

name: Sodium hydrogencarbonate
solubility: soluble (about 9.6 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White powder known outside the laboratory as baking soda. It is an acid salt: the carbonic acid it came from gave away only one of its two hydrogens. Fizzes with acids to give carbon dioxide, and unlike most acid–base reactions that combination takes heat IN rather than giving it out.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium bicarbonate

name: Copper(II) oxide
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Black insoluble powder and a typical basic oxide: it will not dissolve in water, but it dissolves readily in an acid to give a salt and water. Watching black powder disappear into a blue-green solution is one of the clearest demonstrations that a metal oxide neutralises an acid.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Copper(II) oxide

name: Ammonium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 37 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The salt of a strong acid and a weak base, so its solution is acidic rather than neutral. Warming it with any alkali releases ammonia gas, which is the standard laboratory test for an ammonium salt.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonium chloride

name: Carbon dioxide
solubility: slightly soluble (about 0.17 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless, odourless gas given off whenever an acid meets a carbonate or a hydrogencarbonate. It does not burn and does not support burning, so it puts a lighted splint out. The standard test for it is that it turns limewater milky. It is denser than air, so it can collect in the bottom of a container.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Carbon dioxide

name: Ammonia
solubility: very soluble (about 52 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell, released when an ammonium salt is warmed with an alkali. It is the only common alkaline gas, which is why damp red litmus turning blue identifies it. Extremely soluble in water, where it forms a weakly alkaline solution.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonia

name: Calcium chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 75 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left when marble chips or any other calcium carbonate dissolve in hydrochloric acid. Essentially neutral, being the salt of a strong acid and a strong base. It absorbs water strongly, which is why the dry solid is used to keep other chemicals dry.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Calcium chloride

name: Sodium sulfate solution
solubility: soluble (about 19 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless neutral solution formed when sodium hydroxide is neutralised by sulfuric acid. Being the salt of a strong acid and a strong base it is neutral, which is why the end point of that titration sits at pH 7.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium sulfate

name: Copper(II) chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 76 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Blue-green solution formed when black copper(II) oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid. The colour comes from the copper(II) ion, and it is closer to green than copper(II) sulfate's pure blue because the chloride ions also attach to the copper. Acidic, because the copper(II) ion reacts with water.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Copper(II) chloride

name: Barium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 36 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless neutral solution kept for one job above all others: it is the reagent used to test for the sulfate ion, because barium sulfate is one of the most insoluble salts there is. Soluble barium salts are poisonous and must never be tasted or left where they can be mistaken for something harmless.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Barium chloride

name: Potassium bromide solution
solubility: very soluble (about 68 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless neutral solution of a soluble bromide, the salt of a strong acid and a strong base. Used alongside a chloride and an iodide to show that silver nitrate tells the three halides apart by the colour of the precipitate each one gives.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium bromide

name: Iron(III) chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 92 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Yellow-brown solution containing iron in its higher oxidation state, iron(III). Distinctly acidic even though it is a salt, because the small, highly charged Fe³⁺ ion pulls hard on water molecules and releases hydrogen ions. Its colour alone helps tell it from the pale green iron(II) solutions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(III) chloride

name: Barium sulfate
solubility: almost completely insoluble (about 0.00024 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Dense white solid, and one of the most insoluble salts known — which is exactly why the white precipitate it forms is a reliable test for the sulfate ion. Its insolubility is also why it is safe to swallow as a barium meal for X-rays even though soluble barium salts are poisonous: it passes straight through without dissolving.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Barium sulfate

name: Silver iodide
solubility: almost completely insoluble (far less than 0.001 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Yellow solid that drops out when silver nitrate meets any soluble iodide. It is the most strongly coloured of the three silver halides, and the least soluble, so the yellow appears immediately and thickly. Like the other silver halides it darkens in light as silver metal forms.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Silver iodide

name: Silver bromide
solubility: almost completely insoluble (about 0.000014 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Cream-coloured solid formed when silver nitrate meets a soluble bromide. Its colour sits deliberately between the white of silver chloride and the yellow of silver iodide, which is what makes the three halide tests distinguishable. It is very sensitive to light, and was the light-sensitive material in photographic film.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Silver bromide

name: Copper(II) hydroxide
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Pale blue jelly-like precipitate formed when an alkali is added to any copper(II) solution. Its distinctive blue is the standard way of identifying the copper(II) ion. On warming it breaks down to black copper(II) oxide, losing water.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Copper(II) hydroxide

name: Iron(II) hydroxide
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.0006 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Dull green precipitate formed when an alkali is added to an iron(II) solution — the standard test for the iron(II) ion. Left standing in air it slowly turns brown at the surface as oxygen converts iron(II) to iron(III), which is a good demonstration of how easily iron changes between its two oxidation states.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(II) hydroxide

name: Iron(III) hydroxide
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Reddish-brown precipitate formed when an alkali is added to an iron(III) solution — the standard test for the iron(III) ion, and impossible to confuse with the dull green of iron(II). This is essentially the same substance as the rust that forms on iron left in damp air.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(III) hydroxide

name: Magnesium hydroxide
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.0009 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White precipitate formed when an alkali is added to a magnesium solution. Because it is a weak base that is almost insoluble, a suspension of it is mild enough to swallow — it is sold as milk of magnesia to neutralise excess stomach acid.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Magnesium hydroxide

name: Lead(II) chloride
solubility: only slightly soluble (about 0.99 g per 100 mL at 20 °C, and far more in hot water)
description: White solid that appears when a lead solution meets a chloride. It is the exception that makes the chloride solubility rule worth stating carefully: nearly all chlorides are soluble, but the lead, silver and mercury(I) ones are not. Unusually it dissolves in hot water and comes back out as glittering needles on cooling.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Lead(II) chloride

name: Oxygen
solubility: slightly soluble (about 0.9 mg per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless, odourless gas making up about a fifth of the air. It does not burn itself but it supports burning, so a glowing splint bursts back into flame in it — that is the standard test for oxygen. It is the oxidising agent in every combustion and in the rusting of iron.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Oxygen

name: Chlorine water
solubility: soluble (about 0.7 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Chlorine gas dissolved in water, used instead of the gas itself because it is far safer to handle. Very pale yellow-green, and acidic because some of the chlorine reacts with the water. Chlorine is the most reactive of the three common halogens, so it displaces both bromine and iodine from their salts.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Chlorine

name: Bromine water
solubility: soluble (about 3.4 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Bromine dissolved in water, a distinctive orange-brown that makes it easy to see when it is formed or used up. Bromine sits between chlorine and iodine in Group 7: it can displace iodine from an iodide, but chlorine displaces it in turn.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Bromine

name: Iodine solution
solubility: only slightly soluble in water (about 0.03 g per 100 mL at 20 °C), much more soluble in potassium iodide solution
description: Iodine dissolved in water, brown in colour. Iodine barely dissolves in water on its own, so laboratory iodine solution is normally made up in potassium iodide, which dissolves it readily. It is the least reactive of the three common halogens, so it cannot displace either chlorine or bromine.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iodine

name: Potassium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 34 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless neutral solution left behind when chlorine displaces bromine or iodine from their potassium salts. The salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so its solution is neutral.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium chloride

name: Potassium bromide solution
solubility: very soluble (about 68 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless neutral solution formed when bromine displaces iodine from a potassium iodide solution. Chemically the same substance as the bottled potassium bromide on the shelf; this entry is the form that appears as a reaction product.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium bromide

name: Rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide)
solubility: insoluble in water
description: The flaky reddish-brown solid formed when iron is attacked by oxygen and water together. Unlike most compounds it has no fixed formula: the amount of water locked into it varies, which is why it is written Fe2O3·xH2O and why the molar mass given here is that of the Fe2O3 unit alone. Rust flakes away instead of forming a sealed layer, so the iron underneath keeps corroding — which is exactly why iron must be painted, greased or galvanised.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass and density of Fe2O3); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, corrosion and its prevention

name: Sodium chloride (solid)
solubility: soluble (about 36 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Ordinary salt as the dry solid. It does NOT conduct electricity like this, because although it is made of ions those ions are locked in place in the crystal and cannot move. Melt it at about 801 °C, or dissolve it, and the ions become free to move and it conducts well. That contrast is the whole reason solids, melts and solutions behave so differently in electrolysis.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, melting point, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium chloride

name: Sodium metal
solubility: reacts violently with water rather than dissolving
description: Soft silvery metal, so reactive that it is stored under oil and never handled with bare hands. It cannot be obtained by displacement from a solution — anything reactive enough to push sodium out of its salt would itself react with the water first — so the only way to get it is electrolysis of the molten salt. It is less dense than water, which is why it floats and skates across the surface when it reacts.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, extraction of sodium by the Down's cell

name: Chlorine gas
solubility: soluble (about 0.7 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Choking pale yellow-green gas, denser than air and poisonous to breathe. It is given off at the anode whenever a chloride is electrolysed, and it bleaches damp litmus paper — which is how it is identified. It must only ever be produced in a fume cupboard or a very well ventilated room.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Chlorine

name: Sodium hydroxide solution
solubility: very soluble (about 109 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Strongly alkaline solution left behind in the cell when brine is electrolysed. Chemically the same substance as the bottled sodium hydroxide on the shelf; this entry is the form that appears as a reaction product. Producing it this way, alongside chlorine and hydrogen, is one of the largest chemical industries in the world.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, the electrolysis of brine

name: Sulfur powder
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Bright yellow non-metal powder. It burns in air with a distinctive blue flame to give sulfur dioxide. Sulfur present as an impurity in coal and oil is the main source of the sulfur dioxide that causes acid rain, which is why fuels are treated to remove it. Written here as S for simplicity; the element is really made of S8 rings.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, air pollutants

name: Carbon (charcoal)
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Black solid non-metal, the main element in coal, charcoal and wood. Burning it in plenty of air gives carbon dioxide; burning it where air is short gives carbon monoxide instead, which is the poisonous gas responsible for deaths from badly ventilated heaters.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, combustion and air pollutants

name: Nitrogen
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 1.9 mg per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless, odourless gas making up about 78 per cent of the air. Its two atoms are held by a triple bond, which is extremely hard to break — that is why nitrogen is so unreactive that it can be used to keep food and chemicals from reacting with air. Only at the temperature of a lightning strike or a car engine will it combine with oxygen.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, composition of air

name: Sulfur dioxide
solubility: very soluble (about 11 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell like a struck match. It is the main cause of acid rain: released when sulfur-containing coal and oil are burned, it dissolves in cloud droplets to make an acid. It also bleaches damp coloured petals, which is one way of identifying it.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sulfur dioxide

name: Sulfurous acid
solubility: exists only in solution
description: The acid formed when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water, and one of the two acids in acid rain. It is a weak acid and cannot be isolated as a pure liquid — it exists only while it is dissolved. In the air it is slowly oxidised further to sulfuric acid, which is stronger still and does the greater damage.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, acid rain

name: Carbonic acid
solubility: exists only in solution
description: The very weak acid formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water. It is why ordinary clean rain is already slightly acidic at about pH 5.6, before any pollution is involved — so acid rain means rain more acidic than that, not simply rain that is acidic. It is also what makes fizzy drinks taste sharp.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, natural acidity of rain

name: Nitrogen monoxide
solubility: slightly soluble (about 0.006 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless gas made when nitrogen and oxygen are forced together at the temperature of a lightning strike or a car engine. It is easy to spot because the moment it meets air it turns brown, combining with oxygen to make nitrogen dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Nitric oxide

name: Nitrogen dioxide
solubility: soluble, reacting with the water as it dissolves
description: Choking reddish-brown gas, and the only common coloured gas in this laboratory — the brown haze over a congested city is largely this. It is poisonous, attacks the lungs, and dissolves in rain to make nitric acid, so it is the second major cause of acid rain after sulfur dioxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Nitrogen dioxide

name: Nitric acid solution
solubility: miscible
description: Nitric acid as it forms in the atmosphere when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain. Chemically the same substance as the bottled nitric acid on the shelf; this entry is the form that appears as a reaction product, and in real rain it is far more dilute than anything kept in a bottle.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, acid rain

name: Calcium hydrogencarbonate solution (temporary hard water)
solubility: exists only in solution
description: What makes water TEMPORARILY hard. It forms when rainwater carrying dissolved carbon dioxide trickles through limestone and slowly dissolves it. The word temporary is the important part: simply boiling the water breaks this compound down again and the hardness disappears — leaving the limescale behind in the kettle.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, hardness of water

name: Calcium sulfate solution (permanent hard water)
solubility: only slightly soluble (about 0.24 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: What makes water PERMANENTLY hard. Unlike calcium hydrogencarbonate it is not broken down by boiling, so this hardness stays however long the water is heated. Removing it needs a chemical instead — washing soda, which precipitates the calcium out as insoluble calcium carbonate.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, hardness of water

name: Hydrogen peroxide solution
solubility: miscible
description: Colourless liquid that looks exactly like water but slowly falls apart into water and oxygen on its own. Adding a catalyst makes that happen fast enough to watch, which is why it is the standard way of preparing oxygen in a laboratory and the standard demonstration of what a catalyst does.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Hydrogen peroxide

name: Manganese(IV) oxide
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Black powder used as a catalyst. It speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and of potassium chlorate without being used up itself — weigh it before and after and the mass is unchanged, which is the defining test of a catalyst. It can be filtered out at the end and used again.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Reaction Kinetics, catalysis

name: Vanadium(V) oxide
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 0.8 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Orange-yellow solid, the catalyst used in the Contact process for making sulfuric acid. It works by being reduced and then re-oxidised over and over, so it takes a real chemical part in the reaction and yet ends up exactly as it began — which is what a catalyst does.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Contact process

name: Platinum gauze
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Very unreactive silvery metal, used as a catalyst in the form of a fine gauze so that as much surface as possible is exposed. Its job in the Ostwald process is to let ammonia and oxygen meet on its surface; it is expensive, but because a catalyst is not used up the same gauze serves for a very long time.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Ostwald process

name: Sulfur trioxide
solubility: reacts violently with water rather than simply dissolving
description: Colourless gas made in the Contact process by oxidising sulfur dioxide. Adding it straight to water is so violent that it produces a choking mist of acid droplets instead of a solution, which is why industry dissolves it in concentrated sulfuric acid first and then dilutes that.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sulfur trioxide

name: Sulfuric acid solution
solubility: miscible
description: Sulfuric acid as it comes out of the Contact process. Chemically the same substance as the bottled sulfuric acid on the shelf; this entry is the form that appears as a reaction product. More of it is made than of any other chemical in the world.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solution density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry

name: Potassium chlorate
solubility: soluble (about 7 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid rich in oxygen, which it gives up when heated. Heated on its own it needs a fierce flame; with a little manganese(IV) oxide mixed in it releases oxygen at a much lower temperature, which is one of the clearest demonstrations of what a catalyst is for.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium chlorate

name: Potassium chloride (solid)
solubility: soluble (about 34 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid left in the tube after potassium chlorate has given up its oxygen. Like any ionic solid it does not conduct while its ions are locked in the crystal, though it does once dissolved or melted.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium chloride

name: Ammonium chloride (solid)
solubility: soluble (about 37 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Fine white solid that appears as a dense smoke when ammonia gas meets hydrogen chloride gas. The smoke is simply a cloud of tiny solid particles hanging in the air — two invisible gases meeting and producing something you can see is what makes the demonstration memorable.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonium chloride

name: Ammonia solution
solubility: miscible
description: Ammonia dissolved in water, with the sharp smell of the gas still on it. It is a WEAK base: only a small fraction of it takes a hydrogen ion from the water at any moment, so it is alkaline but nowhere near as strongly as sodium hydroxide of the same concentration. That difference between weak and strong, rather than dilute and concentrated, is one of the ideas this bottle is here to teach.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Acids and bases, strong and weak

name: Sodium carbonate (solid)
solubility: soluble (about 21 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid left behind when sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated — washing soda from baking soda. This is the step that turns the cheaper hydrogencarbonate into the carbonate the Solvay process is built to supply, and the same change that makes a cake rise, since the carbon dioxide driven off is what does the lifting.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Solvay process

name: Ammonium nitrate
solubility: very soluble (about 192 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid used as a nitrogen fertiliser. Dissolving it takes in so much heat from its surroundings that the beaker turns genuinely cold to hold — which is what an instant cold pack for a sports injury contains.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, enthalpy of solution +25.7 kJ/mol); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonium nitrate

name: Ammonium nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 192 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left after ammonium nitrate dissolves. Slightly acidic, because it is the salt of a strong acid and a weak base.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonium nitrate

name: Potassium nitrate
solubility: soluble (about 32 g per 100 mL at 20 °C, and far more in hot water)
description: White solid, once called saltpetre. Dissolving it cools the water, though less sharply than ammonium nitrate. Its solubility rises steeply with temperature, which makes it the standard salt for showing how a hot saturated solution crystallises as it cools.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, enthalpy of solution +34.9 kJ/mol); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium nitrate

name: Calcium chloride (anhydrous)
solubility: very soluble (about 75 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid with a strong appetite for water — which is why it is used as a drying agent in desiccators. Dissolving it gives out a lot of heat, enough to make the beaker uncomfortably warm, and that is the chemistry inside a reusable hand warmer.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, enthalpy of solution −81.3 kJ/mol); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Calcium chloride

name: Sodium hydroxide pellets
solubility: very soluble (about 109 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White pellets that attack skin badly and also pull water straight out of the air, so they are weighed quickly and never handled with bare hands. Dissolving them releases a great deal of heat — enough that dissolving a large amount in a small volume can make the solution boil.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, enthalpy of solution −44.5 kJ/mol); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium hydroxide

name: Calcium oxide (quicklime)
solubility: reacts with water rather than dissolving
description: White solid made industrially by roasting limestone in a kiln at about 900 °C. Adding water to it — slaking — is one of the most violently exothermic reactions a school ever demonstrates: the lump cracks apart, steam rises off it, and the water can reach boiling point on its own.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, exothermic reactions

name: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
solubility: soluble (about 20 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The white powder left when blue copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated and lose their water. It is the standard chemical test for water: add even a trace of water and the white turns blue at once. The test says water is present, but not that it is pure — distilled water and tap water both turn it blue.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, test for water

name: Copper(II) sulfate crystals
solubility: soluble (about 32 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The familiar blue crystals. The blue comes entirely from water built into the crystal itself — five molecules of it for every copper sulfate — which is called water of crystallisation. Drive that water off with heat and the blue goes with it, leaving a white powder.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — water of crystallisation

name: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride
solubility: very soluble (about 53 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Blue solid, and the other standard test for water: paper soaked in it and dried turns from blue to pink the moment water touches it. Because the change reverses on drying, the same paper can be used again, and the colour is also used in novelty humidity indicators.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, test for water

name: Cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate
solubility: very soluble (about 76 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The pink hydrated form of cobalt(II) chloride, holding six water molecules in its crystal. Warming it drives the water off and it returns to blue — the pink and blue pair is the clearest demonstration there is that water of crystallisation is what a hydrate's colour depends on.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — water of crystallisation

name: Ammonium chloride solution
solubility: soluble (about 37 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left after ammonium chloride dissolves, which it does while taking heat in from its surroundings. Acidic rather than neutral, being the salt of a strong acid and a weak base.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility, enthalpy of solution +14.8 kJ/mol); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Ammonium chloride

name: Silver metal
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Bright unreactive metal, the best conductor of electricity of any element. It sits at the bottom of the electrochemical series with a standard electrode potential of +0.80 V, which is why nothing common displaces it from solution and why it does not tarnish in air or dissolve in dilute acids. That unreactivity is exactly why it has been used for coins and jewellery for thousands of years.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, standard electrode potential +0.7996 V); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry

name: Lead metal
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Soft, heavy, dull grey metal. Its standard electrode potential is −0.13 V, placing it just above hydrogen and below copper — so it displaces copper and silver from their solutions but cannot displace zinc or iron. Lead is a cumulative poison, which is why lead water pipes and leaded petrol were both phased out.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, standard electrode potential −0.1262 V); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry

name: Copper(II) nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 145 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Blue solution formed when copper displaces silver from silver nitrate. Watching a colourless solution turn blue while silver crystals grow on the copper is the clearest sign that the copper is dissolving as it pushes the silver out.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Copper(II) nitrate

name: Zinc nitrate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 120 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution left when zinc displaces a less reactive metal from its nitrate. Mildly acidic, because the zinc ion reacts weakly with water.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Zinc nitrate

name: Aluminium oxide (bauxite)
solubility: insoluble in water
description: White solid, the ore aluminium is extracted from. It melts at over 2000 °C, which made aluminium a precious metal until it was discovered that dissolving the oxide in molten cryolite brings the working temperature down to about 950 °C. Aluminium is far too reactive to be extracted by heating with carbon the way iron is, so electrolysis is the only route.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, melting point); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, extraction of aluminium

name: Aluminium metal
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Light silvery metal produced by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide. Its electrode potential of −1.66 V says it should be violently reactive, and yet aluminium windows and pans last for years — because it grows an unbroken skin of oxide the instant it meets air, and that layer seals the metal underneath. Rust, by contrast, flakes off and leaves the iron exposed.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, standard electrode potential −1.662 V); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry

name: Lithium metal
solubility: reacts with water rather than dissolving
description: The first alkali metal, and the least dense solid element there is — at 0.53 g/mL it floats high on water. It is the least reactive of the alkali metals, which is why it fizzes gently in water where sodium melts and potassium catches fire. It is also the only one of the three that burns in air to the simple oxide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements

name: Potassium metal
solubility: reacts violently with water rather than dissolving
description: Soft silvery metal, stored under oil like sodium and even more reactive. Its outer electron is further from the nucleus than sodium's and more easily lost, which is why reactivity increases down Group I rather than decreasing. In water it reacts so fast that the hydrogen produced catches fire, burning with the lilac flame that identifies potassium.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements

name: Lithium hydroxide solution
solubility: soluble (about 13 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Strongly alkaline solution left after lithium reacts with water. It is the least soluble of the Group I hydroxides — the odd one out in a group whose hydroxides otherwise dissolve freely.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Lithium hydroxide

name: Potassium hydroxide solution
solubility: very soluble (about 112 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Strongly alkaline solution left after potassium reacts with water, also called caustic potash. Chemically it behaves almost exactly like sodium hydroxide, which is what you would expect from the element directly below sodium in the same group.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Potassium hydroxide

name: Lithium oxide
solubility: reacts with water to give the hydroxide
description: White solid, and the point of interest is that it exists at all: lithium is the ONLY alkali metal that burns in air to the plain oxide. Sodium gives the peroxide and potassium the superoxide instead, so a group whose members are supposed to behave alike parts company the moment they meet oxygen.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA, reactions with oxygen

name: Sodium peroxide
solubility: reacts with water
description: Pale yellow solid containing the peroxide ion, with its oxygen–oxygen bond intact. Burning sodium in plenty of air gives this rather than the simple oxide, which is the first sign that the alkali metals stop behaving identically as you go down the group. It is used in submarines and breathing apparatus because it reacts with exhaled carbon dioxide and gives back oxygen.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA, reactions with oxygen

name: Magnesium carbonate
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.01 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White insoluble solid. It decomposes on heating at about 350 °C — low enough to do in a school test tube, unlike calcium carbonate which needs a kiln. That difference is the Group II trend in one experiment: thermal stability of the carbonates increases going down the group.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, decomposition temperature); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, thermal stability of carbonates

name: Barium carbonate
solubility: almost insoluble (about 0.002 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White insoluble solid, the least soluble and the most thermally stable of the Group II carbonates — it needs above 1300 °C to decompose, against magnesium carbonate's 350 °C. Both trends run the same way down the group, which is the pattern this part of the syllabus exists to establish.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, decomposition temperature); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA

name: Sodium bromide
solubility: very soluble (about 91 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid, indistinguishable by eye from sodium chloride. What separates them is how they behave with concentrated sulfuric acid: the chloride simply gives off hydrogen chloride, while the bromide is oxidised and orange bromine appears. That difference is the reducing power of the halide ion showing itself.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of halides

name: Sodium iodide
solubility: very soluble (about 184 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: White solid, and the strongest reducing agent of the three common halides. With concentrated sulfuric acid it does not stop at giving off hydrogen iodide — it drives the sulfur all the way down to hydrogen sulfide, with its unmistakable rotten-egg smell, and leaves purple iodine behind.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of halides

name: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach)
solubility: very soluble (about 29 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The active ingredient of household bleach, made by passing chlorine into cold sodium hydroxide. It is alkaline, not acidic, which surprises people. It is also the reason two warnings are printed on every bottle: mixed with an acid it releases chlorine, and mixed with an ammonia-based cleaner it releases chloramine. Both are genuinely dangerous and both happen in ordinary kitchens.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of chlorine with alkalis

name: Manganese(II) chloride solution
solubility: very soluble (about 72 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Very pale pink solution left in the flask after manganese(IV) oxide has been used to make chlorine. The manganese has been reduced from the +4 state to +2, which is the other half of the redox: the oxide oxidises the chloride to chlorine and is itself reduced.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Manganese(II) chloride

name: Sodium hydrogensulfate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 50 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The salt left when sulfuric acid gives away only one of its two hydrogens. It is an ACID salt: the hydrogen it still holds makes its solution genuinely acidic at about pH 1, which is a useful reminder that being a salt does not mean being neutral.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Sodium bisulfate

name: Hydrogen chloride gas
solubility: extremely soluble (about 72 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless gas that fumes in moist air, because it grabs water vapour and forms a mist of hydrochloric acid droplets. Dry hydrogen chloride gas does NOT behave as an acid at all — it will not turn dry litmus red — which is the classic demonstration that an acid needs water to release its hydrogen ions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Hydrogen chloride

name: Hydrogen sulfide
solubility: soluble (about 0.4 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The rotten-egg gas. It is far more dangerous than its smell suggests, because at higher concentrations it deadens the sense of smell within minutes — so the warning disappears exactly when the danger is greatest. Its appearance when sodium iodide meets concentrated sulfuric acid is the sign that the iodide has reduced the sulfur all the way from +6 to −2.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Hydrogen sulfide

name: Diamminesilver(I) solution
solubility: soluble
description: The colourless solution formed when silver chloride dissolves in ammonia. Two ammonia molecules attach themselves to the silver ion, holding it in solution as a complex ion — which is how a precipitate that would not dissolve in water can be made to disappear. Silver bromide needs concentrated ammonia to do the same, and silver iodide will not dissolve at all.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, distinguishing the silver halides

name: Chloramine vapour
solubility: soluble
description: Colourless, sharply irritating vapour formed when bleach meets ammonia. It attacks the eyes and airways, and because both liquids are ordinary household cleaners this is one of the commonest ways people are accidentally poisoned at home. This entry exists to teach why the two must never be mixed, not how to make it.
source: PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Chloramine; Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of hypochlorites

name: Potassium thiocyanate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 217 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Colourless solution kept for one job: it is the most sensitive test there is for the iron(III) ion. Even a trace turns it blood red, which makes it useful for detecting rust in water. It is also the standard demonstration of an equilibrium shifting, because adding more of either reactant deepens the colour visibly.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, complex formation

name: Thiocyanatoiron(III) complex
solubility: soluble
description: The intense blood-red complex formed when a thiocyanate ion attaches to an iron(III) ion. The colour is far stronger than either starting solution, which is what makes the test so sensitive. Colour this deep from a complex ion is characteristic of the transition metals and is the reason they are the coloured part of the periodic table.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, complex ions and colour

name: Tetraamminecopper(II) sulfate solution
solubility: soluble
description: The deep royal blue formed when four ammonia molecules replace the water around a copper(II) ion. Set it against ordinary copper(II) sulfate's pale blue and the difference is startling — same metal, same oxidation state, different ligands, completely different colour. That is the clearest evidence there is that in a transition metal complex the colour belongs to the whole ion, not to the metal alone.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, complex formation and ligand exchange

name: Potassium dichromate solution
solubility: soluble (about 12 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Bright orange solution and a powerful oxidising agent in acid, where the chromium is in its +6 state. Add alkali and it turns yellow as it converts to the chromate — the same chromium, a different ion, a different colour. Chromium(VI) compounds are toxic and cause cancer, so they are handled with care and are being phased out of industry.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, oxidation states of chromium

name: Sodium chromate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 84 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Yellow solution containing the chromate ion. It holds chromium in exactly the same +6 state as the orange dichromate — nothing has been oxidised or reduced in going from one to the other, only rearranged. Add acid and the orange comes straight back, which makes the pair a clean demonstration that colour depends on the whole ion rather than on oxidation state alone.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, the chromate–dichromate equilibrium

name: Chromium(III) sulfate solution
solubility: soluble (about 62 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Green solution holding chromium in the +3 state, which is what orange dichromate becomes once it has been reduced. Watching orange turn green is the standard way of seeing dichromate act as an oxidising agent — and it is the same colour change used in the old breathalyser, where alcohol reduced the dichromate on the tube.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, variable oxidation states

name: Chromium(III) hydroxide
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Grey-green gelatinous precipitate formed when alkali is added to a chromium(III) solution — the test for that ion. It is amphoteric: it dissolves in excess alkali as well as in acid, which is behaviour a simple metal hydroxide like magnesium's does not show.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, chromium chemistry

name: Potassium permanganate solution
solubility: soluble (about 6.4 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Intensely purple solution, so strongly coloured that a very dilute one still looks deep. Manganese here is in its highest oxidation state, +7, which makes it a powerful oxidising agent. Its colour is its own indicator: in an acidic titration the purple is destroyed as it reacts, so the first faint pink that persists marks the end point and no separate indicator is needed.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, oxidation states of manganese

name: Manganese(II) sulfate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 52 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: So faintly pink that in a titration it reads as colourless — which is exactly what makes potassium permanganate self-indicating. The manganese has fallen from +7 all the way to +2, a change of five oxidation states in one step, and taken its intense purple with it.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Manganese(II) sulfate

name: Iron(III) sulfate solution
solubility: soluble (about 44 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Yellow-brown solution holding iron in the +3 state, formed when pale green iron(II) is oxidised. Distinctly acidic, because the small highly charged Fe³⁺ ion pulls hard on surrounding water molecules and releases hydrogen ions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Iron(III) sulfate

name: Potassium manganate
solubility: soluble, decomposing in water
description: Dark green solid holding manganese in the +6 state — one step down from the +7 of permanganate. Manganese is the clearest example of a transition metal's variable oxidation states: purple at +7, green at +6, black as the +4 oxide, and very pale pink at +2, each with its own colour.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, oxidation states of manganese

name: Methane
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 2.2 mg per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The simplest alkane and the main component of natural gas. Its four hydrogens point to the corners of a tetrahedron, not a square — the shape a carbon atom with four single bonds always takes. Being saturated, it has no double bond for anything to add across, so it reacts only by substitution and then only when forced with ultraviolet light.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, alkanes

name: Ethane
solubility: very slightly soluble (about 6 mg per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The two-carbon alkane, and the saturated partner to ethene. Every bond is a single bond, so it is the control in the bromine water test: shake it with bromine water in the dark and nothing whatever happens, which is exactly what makes the test for unsaturation mean something.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, alkanes

name: Ethene (ethylene)
solubility: slightly soluble (about 13 mg per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The simplest alkene, and the single most important organic chemical made industrially — the starting point for polythene, ethanol, antifreeze and much else. Its carbon–carbon DOUBLE bond makes the whole molecule flat and gives it the reactivity alkanes lack: things add ACROSS the double bond rather than substituting into it. Plants also release it as the hormone that ripens fruit.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, alkenes

name: Ethyne (acetylene)
solubility: soluble (about 0.1 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The simplest alkyne. Its carbon–carbon TRIPLE bond holds the whole molecule in a straight line, and means it can take on twice as much bromine as ethene can — which is how the bromine water test tells an alkyne from an alkene rather than merely spotting that something is unsaturated. Burned with oxygen it gives the hottest common flame, over 3000 °C, which is what an oxy-acetylene torch cuts steel with.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, alkynes

name: Calcium carbide
solubility: reacts with water rather than dissolving
description: Grey solid that reacts with water to give ethyne, which is how the gas is made in a laboratory and how miners' carbide lamps once worked. It must be kept absolutely dry — moisture in the air is enough to start it slowly. It is still sold in some countries to ripen fruit artificially, a use that is banned in many places because of the arsenic and phosphorus impurities it usually carries.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, preparation of ethyne

name: Chloromethane
solubility: slightly soluble (about 0.5 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Methane with one hydrogen replaced by chlorine — the first product of free radical substitution. The trouble with the reaction is that it does not stop here: the chloromethane is itself attacked, giving dichloromethane, then trichloromethane, then tetrachloromethane, so the real product is always a mixture. That lack of control is why free radical substitution is a poor way to make one particular compound.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, halogenation of alkanes

name: 1,2-dibromoethane
solubility: almost insoluble in water (about 0.4 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The colourless product of adding bromine across the double bond of ethene. One bromine atom goes to each carbon — hence 1,2 — and the double bond becomes a single bond. Because the product is colourless, the orange of the bromine water simply disappears, which is what makes the test so easy to read.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, addition reactions of alkenes

name: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane
solubility: almost insoluble in water
description: What ethyne gives with bromine: FOUR bromine atoms, not two, because a triple bond can add twice over. Measuring how much bromine a sample takes up therefore tells you not just that it is unsaturated but how unsaturated — the principle behind the iodine number used to grade fats and oils.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, addition reactions of alkynes

name: Ethanol
solubility: miscible
description: The alcohol in drinks, and industrially made by adding water across the double bond of ethene. Its OH group lets it hydrogen bond, which is why a two-carbon molecule that ought to be a gas is a liquid, and why it mixes with water in any proportion while ethane does not dissolve at all. It does not conduct: the OH hydrogen is held far too tightly to come off as an ion, so ethanol is not an acid.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols; Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, hydration of alkenes

name: Ethane-1,2-diol (glycol)
solubility: miscible
description: A diol — two OH groups, one on each carbon — formed when cold dilute potassium permanganate attacks a double bond. With two chances to hydrogen bond it is thick, high boiling and completely mixable with water, which is what makes it the antifreeze in car radiators. It tastes sweet and is seriously poisonous, a combination that makes it dangerous to animals and children.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, oxidation of alkenes

name: Nickel catalyst
solubility: insoluble in water
description: Finely divided silvery metal, the catalyst used to add hydrogen across carbon–carbon multiple bonds. It is chosen over platinum for industry simply because it is far cheaper while doing the same job. This is the catalyst that hardens liquid vegetable oils into margarine, by hydrogenating the double bonds in their chains.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, catalytic hydrogenation

name: Phosphoric acid
solubility: miscible
description: A tribasic acid — three hydrogens it can give away — but a WEAK one, which is why its solution is nowhere near as acidic as hydrochloric acid of the same concentration. It is the catalyst for hydrating ethene to ethanol industrially, and, more familiarly, it is what gives cola drinks their sharp taste.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, industrial hydration of ethene

name: Benzene
solubility: almost insoluble in water (about 0.18 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: A flat ring of six carbons whose six spare electrons are spread evenly right round it rather than sitting in three separate double bonds. That delocalisation is why the ring is unusually stable, why every carbon–carbon bond in it is exactly the same length, and why benzene refuses to behave like an alkene. It is also a proven carcinogen, which is why it has been replaced by methylbenzene in most school laboratories.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, structure of benzene

name: Iron(III) bromide
solubility: very soluble (about 490 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Dark solid used as the halogen carrier that lets bromine attack a benzene ring. Its job is to polarise the bromine molecule enough to make one end strongly positive, because plain bromine is nowhere near reactive enough to touch a ring as stable as benzene. Without it, benzene and bromine water simply sit together doing nothing.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, halogenation of benzene

name: Bromobenzene
solubility: almost insoluble in water
description: Benzene with one hydrogen swapped for a bromine — and the ring is still intact. That is the point: the bromine SUBSTITUTED rather than adding across a bond, because breaking the delocalised ring would cost more energy than the reaction gains.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, electrophilic substitution

name: Nitrobenzene
solubility: almost insoluble in water (about 0.19 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Pale yellow oily liquid smelling of almonds — a smell that is a genuinely dangerous invitation, because it is absorbed straight through the skin and poisons the blood's ability to carry oxygen. It is the starting point for aniline and from there for a great many dyes, which is how the synthetic dye industry began.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, nitration of benzene

name: Benzenesulfonic acid
solubility: very soluble
description: A strong acid built onto a benzene ring, and unlike benzene itself it dissolves freely in water. That combination — a water-loving acidic head on a water-hating hydrocarbon tail — is exactly the structure of a detergent, which is what sulfonation is done for industrially.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, sulfonation of benzene

name: Cyclohexane
solubility: almost insoluble in water
description: The fully saturated six-carbon ring, and what benzene becomes once it has been forced to take on hydrogen. It is NOT flat: with every carbon tetrahedral the ring puckers into a chair shape, which is the clearest possible contrast with benzene's rigidly planar ring.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, hydrogenation of benzene

name: Bromoethane
solubility: slightly soluble (about 0.9 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: A halogenoalkane, and one of the most useful starting materials in organic chemistry. The carbon–bromine bond is polar, leaving that carbon slightly positive and open to attack by anything with a lone pair — so bromoethane can be turned into an alcohol, an amine, a nitrile or an alkene depending only on what is attacked with and under what conditions.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alkyl Halides

name: Sodium hydroxide in ethanol
solubility: miscible with ethanol
description: The same sodium hydroxide, dissolved in ethanol instead of water — and that single change of solvent sends bromoethane down a completely different path.
